title: MB0-04302
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: This is the decision for XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX (claimant) a citizen of Saint Vincent, who claims refugee protection in Canada pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA)1.
The Tribunal applied the Chairperson's Guideline 4 on Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-related Persecution.2

The Tribunal noted that the claimant was of limited education. The Tribunal progressed in a slow and deliberate manner ensuring that the claimant understood all of the questions being posed. Regular breaks were offered and counsel was encouraged to support the claimant as needed.

The claimant alleged a fear of her ex-boyfriend whom she identified as XXXXXXX (XXXX). The claimant alleged being in a relationship with him from 2000 through 2001. The claimant alleged that XXXX was abusive so she moved in 2001.
The claimant alleged that she saw XXXX at a grocery store in XXXXXXX 2002 and that he followed her home, kidnapped her and then sexually assaulted her.
She then came to Canada on XXXXX, 2004 and claimed refugee protection on July 5, 2010.

The Tribunal finds that based on the particular circumstances of this case, the claimant's narrative regarding XXX pursuing her since the incident in 2002 and still now in 2012 was not found credible. As such, she is not found to be a "Convention refugee" pursuant to section 96 of IRPA. Nor is she deemed to be a "person in need of protection" pursuant to section 97(1) of IRPA. ANALYSIS Identity

The Tribunal is satisfied by the photocopies of the claimant's Vincentian passport and related documentation originally seized by Citizenship and Immigration Canada (CIC)3 and accepts that she is a citizen of Saint Vincent. Credibility

The claimant testified in a straight-forward manner without any embellishment. At the beginning of the hearing the claimant testified that everything in her documentation was true, accurate, correct and up to date. That being said, there were several inconsistencies and errors in timing and her whereabouts and employment history that overlapped and were confusing. Many modifications were made to the documentation to incorporate corrections. As such, credibility concerns arose throughout her testimony as detailed below:

No credible proof of the existence of the agent of harm or any subsequent threats - Asked for some form of proof to credibly establish the existence of, relationship with, and current whereabouts of XXXX, the claimant could provide none. Asked for proof of their alleged two-year relationship, but nothing was forthcoming. Asked for a picture, or letter or gift that he might have given her during the course of their alleged relationship and the claimant did not have anything. She also could not really recall when exactly they met or started dating. She thinks it was in high school in 2000 or 2001, when she was around seventeen years old, but she was not certain and the dates in the respective port of entry (POE), personal information form (PIF) and her oral testimony were somewhat conflicting. Her explanation being that it was almost a decade ago so she really cannot remember. For someone that the claimant was allegedly with for some time, and alleged a fear for her life from, were she to return to Saint Vincent in 2012, she was able to convey very little information about him.

The Tribunal accepted that the claimant was in a relationship with XXXX, that it was abusive and that it ended in 2001, when she moved from XXXX to XXXXXXX. The Tribunal also accepted that notwithstanding an eight month cessation of the relationship, and nothing to corroborate that XXXX was looking for her, the claimant may have run into XXXX at a grocery store and he may have followed her home as she alleged, then taken her in his car to his apartment and then sexually assaulted her in XXXXXX of 2002. The claimant was given the benefit of the doubt that this alleged incident may have occurred. However, she was asked if XXXX was stalking her or if it was a chance encounter and the claimant testified earnestly that she was not aware of him following her or stalking her. Asked if she reported the assault to the authorities and the claimant testified that she did not. Asked if she sought medical attention after the alleged sexual assault in XXXXXX 2002, but she stated that she was embarrassed and did not seek treatment. Then, subsequent to the alleged assault in XXXXXX of 2002, the claimant alleged moving back to XXXXX and staying with her aunt, who lived in close proximity to where the claimant used to reside. The claimant testified that she got a job working in a XXXXX. Although asked, nothing in the claimant's testimony or documentary evidence credibly conveyed that XXX came after her or looked for her following the alleged incident, in XXXXX 2002, nor has he subsequent to her departure in XXX of 2004. Nor did she credibly convey to the Tribunal that XXX would be looking for her in the future were she to return to Saint Vincent.

Asked if XXXX has contacted any of her family members that continue to reside in Saint Vincent and the claimant answered earnestly that she was not aware of any of her family members (father, mother, brother, or aunt - whom she testified is really the step-daughter of her mother) being contacted, threatened or assaulted by XXXX. Nor did she believe that he has asked them about her whereabouts over the last eight years. The claimant testified that her friends tell her that they still see XXXX around. Asked for an attestation letter or confirmation that XXXX has asked her friends about the claimant's whereabouts but again, nothing was forthcoming. Asked what the claimant knew of XXXX's situation and whether he is married or dating or has children, but she had no information. The claimant failed to credibly establish that XXXX is or would be after her in 2012.

Questionable whereabouts of the claimant - The claimant's PIF materials had overlapping dates of where she allegedly lived and worked. This was addressed during her oral testimony. However, from her explanations, she was allegedly living in XXXX where the agent of harm lived while in a relationship with him. When she left the relationship in 2001, she allegedly moved to XXXXXX. Yet, she testified that she returned to XXXX on the weekends but did not see XXXX. Her explanation being that she did not go out and she only ever traveled at night. The claimant then alleged that after she encountered XXXX on one occasion in XXXXX in XXXXXX 2002, she left her job and moved back to XXXX to her aunt's where she remained, seemingly without any further contact from XXXX until her departure for Canada in 2004. Asked why she would return to XXXX and the claimant testified that she felt safe with her aunt. Asked if XXXX ever came to her aunt's home and the claimant testified that he did not.

The claimant further alleged working in a XXXXXX in XXXX and caring for her aunt's children at the same time in 2003. Then at some point in 2003, she was not certain as to when, but she thinks it was some time between January and June 2003, XXXX's cousin, whose name she did not know, allegedly approached her at work and told her that XXXX was looking for her. Asked if XXXX ever showed up at the XXXXX where she worked in search for her and she testified that XXXX never did. Nothing credibly established to the Tribunal that XXXX was pursuing the claimant in Saint Vincent in 2003, or that he would be, close to a decade later in 2012. Delay in claiming

The Tribunal is sensitive to the alleged situation for women in Saint Vincent. However, further, negatively impacting on the claimant's credibility and subjective fear was the fact that she alleged that the abuse started in 2001. She further alleged a sexual assault in XXXXXX 2002, yet did not leave the country until a year and a half later in XXXX of 2004. Then, when she came to Canada, she waited a further six years before seeking refugee protection. Asked why not leave sooner than 2004 if in fear for her life, but the claimant had no response other than to say she was working. The delay in departure from her country negatively impacted on the claimant's subjective fear.

With regard to the delay in filing a claim for refugee protection in Canada, counsel submitted a letter on the claimant's behalf to address the delay factor due to the claimant allegedly being ill advised by former counsel and/or consultants. The claimant was first allegedly told that she could not file a claim for refugee protection. An application for a visa as a caregiver was commenced but not pursued to completion. Then the claimant allegedly sought out the services of an immigration consultant who started to file a humanitarian and compassionate (H&C) grounds claim on her behalf. Although asked, the claimant never made it clear to the Tribunal what said humanitarian and compassionate grounds were, but regardless, the consultant in question is allegedly no longer in practice and that claim was never filed. The claimant then learned of her current counsel and filed the within application in 2010, six years after arrival in Canada. Asked for proof of the aforementioned caregiver application and/or H&C claim but no documentation was forthcoming. As such, the Tribunal took the word of the claimant and her present counsel and did not hold the delay in filing a refugee protection claim in Canada against the claimant's credibility. Section 96

The Tribunal assessed the claim on the ground of membership in a particular social group, namely women claiming a fear based on gender persecution. The Tribunal recognizes that there is a Domestic Violence Act4 in Saint Vincent, but also notes that violence against women remains a serious problem. However, in the particular circumstances of this case, the Tribunal finds that while there is a nexus to a Convention ground for the claimant, by her own testimony, she never credibly established, to the satisfaction of the Tribunal, that she was being pursued by XXXX in the past, or that she would be pursued by him in the future. The Tribunal gave her the benefit of the doubt that the alleged incidents occurred. However, after December 2002, the claimant did not credibly establish any further contact, threats or well-founded fear of persecution that would support a finding of any prospective fear in 2012 a decade later. Further still, by her own testimony, she never credibly established that she took any steps in her own country to report the alleged agent of harm to any authorities. Nor did she credibly convey to the Tribunal's satisfaction that XXXX has been, is pursuing her, nor that he would pursue her in the future. Simply testifying that her friends see him around was not deemed sufficient in these particular circumstances to credibly establish a well founded fear of persecution. No nexus on the basis of race, religion, nationality or political opinion was found to exist either. Therefore, based on her testimony, the claimant is not deemed to be a "Convention refugee" in this instance. Section 97(1)
There being no other grounds raised other than those mentioned under section 96, the Tribunal finds that the claimant is therefore not a "person in need of protection" either. Section 97(1)(a)

To be clear, the claimant did not allege any risk of torture or that the agent of harm is a State actor, nor that his actions were sanctioned by the State. As such, section 97(1)(a) of IRPA does not apply. Section 97(1)(b)

Given that the claimant only identified her former boyfriend as the alleged agent of harm and solely with regard to his allegedly pursuing her because she is a woman, there being no other grounds and no finding of credibility on the initial basis, no finding of a personal risk of harm or risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment was credibly established by the claimant either. As such, section 97(1)(b) does not apply and the claimant is therefore not found to be a "person in need of protection". State Protection

The Tribunal considered whether or not, there is adequate State protection in Saint Vincent and more specifically in the particular circumstances of this case, whether the claimant provided clear and convincing evidence of the State's inability to protect her. There is a presumption that, except in situations where a State is in a complete breakdown, a State is capable of protecting its citizens. The burden falls on the claimant to rebut the presumption. By her own testimony and available materials, notwithstanding counsel's submission of numerous articles on violence against women in the Caribbean5, and reference during her submission to several Vincentian cases, the claimant failed to credibly establish, to the Tribunal's satisfaction, that reasonable efforts were made to seek State protection nor that it was either not available or inadequate. The articles submitted confirmed what the Tribunal is already cognizant of, a fact that domestic violence continues to be a problem in Saint Vincent. However, in the articles presented6, there is mention of police intervention, arrests and convictions. Asked if the claimant ever went to the police or any higher authority for assistance, she replied that she made one alleged attempt in XXXXX in 2001 wherein she failed to allege abuse. She testified that she told the police that XXXX was a drug dealer. As for the alleged assault in XXXXXXXX in XXXXXX of 2002, when asked if she went to the police, the claimant said that she did. She said she told them her ex-boyfriend followed her home. She testified that the police thought she was making a false accusation. Asked if she pursued the matter or sought a protection order, but she testified that she did not. Asked if she had any copies of the alleged reports but she did not. Asked what efforts were made to obtain corroboration of her allegations but no efforts were made. As such, the claimant failed to take reasonable steps to pursue State protection in her own country. As a result, the alleged agent of harm was never arrested, detained, convicted or jailed. He suffered no sanctions and there is no reason to believe that the agent of harm would pursue the claimant, for any reason, were she to return to her country in 2012.

The National Documentation Package (NDP) on Saint Vincent supports that some protection for victims of domestic abuse does exist and the police receives training. The NDP does however also note that matters of this nature are frequently not pursued by the victims.7 The claimant herself admitted that she never reported the abuse in 2001. In 2002, she allegedly reported but was not found credible. Her aunt allegedly told her to file a report in XXXXX regarding the alleged rape, but the claimant testified that she chose not to do so and no Protection Order or Family Court assistance8 was sought. The claimant just remained in Saint Vincent until XXXX 2004 and then came to Canada. The Tribunal determined that the claimant failed to meet her burden to establish, with clear and convincing evidence, that State protection would not be forthcoming. Asked why she failed to take reasonable steps to seek State protection and her response was that the police do not do anything. She could not say from her own experience. This is just what she allegedly heard around the village.

Failure to use reasonable efforts to seek protection in one's own country prior to seeking protection internationally would, in general, cause an application to fail. The Tribunal appreciates counsel's efforts and the presentation of jurisprudence, namely seven cases where women feared gender persecution. The Tribunal is acutely aware that there are Federal Court decisions that support the notion that adequate State protection is not available in Saint Vincent for women who are victims of rape or domestic abuse. The Tribunal finds however, that one must carefully evaluate and take into account the particulars of each case, based on its own merits, which includes an assessment of the credibility factors and corroborative materials available. The burden of proof is on the claimant to establish either that State protection would not have been reasonably forthcoming or that any efforts to seek protection would have exposed her to an even greater risk. She failed to take reasonable steps to seek protection. She remained in the country for a year and a half after the last alleged attack and was never contacted or located by the alleged agent of harm. As such, the claimant failed to provide the clear and convincing evidence necessary to rebut the presumption of State protection on her own behalf. Notwithstanding that violence against women is acknowledged to be a problem in Saint Vincent, that fact alone is not enough to exempt the claimant from her requirement to pursue reasonable efforts to seek and follow through on a request for State protection.9

In light of the above, although the Tribunal acknowledges that the treatment of women and the support for women who are victims of rape or domestic abuse is not yet ideal10, the Tribunal finds that the claimant has not fulfilled her burden of proof to establish that State protection was not available. Nor did the claimant credibly convey to the Tribunal that there was inadequate State protection in Saint Vincent for her. Simply testifying that she was afraid or that the police do nothing was not deemed sufficient to relieve the claimant of her obligations or the onus to rebut the presumption of State protection. Internal Flight Alternative (IFA)

In the further alternative, even if the claimant's narrative had been found credible that XXXX has been and would be after her in 2012, and if she had credibly established that she sought State protection and that it was not forthcoming or that it was inadequate, an IFA would have been available. In order to determine if there is an IFA, the test to be applied is: (i) if there is another part of the country, where the claimant would not have a well-founded fear of persecution and (ii) that it would not be objectively unreasonable or unduly harsh to expect the claimant to move to this location.

The claimant testified to the Tribunal that her friends have told her that XXXX continues to reside in XXXX. Asked if she could relocate and find a job as a XXXXXXX in Canouan, Fancy, or Georgetown and her response was that she did not think so. She said that there are no jobs available. Asked how she knew this but she could not say. Nor did she credibly establish that it would be unduly harsh for her to return to Saint Vincent and relocate to any of the proposed locations. The claimant was asked but provided no evidence (oral or documentary) or reasonable explanation to refute why one of these locations in Saint Vincent would not be viable. The Tribunal appreciates that the claimant is of limited education, but she failed to explain why she would not be able to find some form of work or a place to live in any of the locations proposed. Notwithstanding that Saint Vincent is notably a small country, the Tribunal held that the claimant failed to credibly establish that XXXX is or would be looking for her. Further, the Tribunal determined that it would not be unduly harsh for her to relocate in any of the proposed areas. As such, both prongs of the test for an IFA have been met.

Based on the totality of the evidence and testimony before it, the Tribunal finds that the claimant's narrative regarding XXXX being after her in 2012 was not deemed credible. It is determined that no one is currently after the claimant, nor would they be, were she to return to Saint Vincent. Further, even if the claimant had credibly established that some one was after her, by her own testimony, reasonable efforts to seek State protection was not credibly established to have been sought. Nor was State protection found to be inadequate in Saint Vincent for the claimant. As such, the Tribunal finds that the claimant is not a "Convention refugee" or a "person in need of protection".

For all of the reasons cited above, the Tribunal rejects the claim for refugee protection.
